meta.title: Who really said "I awoke, only to find that the rest of the world is still asleep"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Leonardo da Vinci never wrote this. It’s a first-person rewrite of Sigmund Freud’s 1910 simile about Leonardo, itself borrowed from novelist Dmitry Merezhkovsky.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I awoke, only to find that the rest of the world is still asleep'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Leonardo da Vinci. The line is an anonymous paraphrase of Freud’s 1910 simile describing Leonardo — a simile Freud credited to Dmitry Merezhkovsky.

answer.label: Not Leonardo da Vinci — a paraphrase of Freud
answer.authorDates: 1856–1939 · Founder of psychoanalysis · borrowed the simile from novelist Dmitry Merezhkovsky
answer.sourceLine: The real sentence is neither first-person nor by Leonardo. In his 1910 study Leonardo da Vinci and a Memory of His Childhood (English trans. 1916), Freud described Leonardo as “a man who awoke too early in the darkness, while the others were all still asleep” — a simile he expressly credited to Dmitry Merezhkovsky. The popular “I awoke…” version is an anonymous modern rewrite found in none of Leonardo’s notebooks. As Leonardo scholar Martin Kemp put it, “about 80% of the Leo ‘quotes’ on the internet are not by him. This is not amongst the 20%.”

source.excerpt: In Merezhkovsky’s admirable simile, he was like a man who had awoken too early in the darkness, while everyone else was still asleep.
trail: Quote aggregators such as Quote Park credit the line to Leonardo while simultaneously flagging it as misattributed and tracing it to Freud.
A 2019 Check Your Fact investigation rated it false; Oxford Leonardo scholar Martin Kemp confirmed the line is not among Leonardo’s genuine words.
The image traces to Freud’s 1910 essay, where he calls it “Merezhkovsky’s admirable simile” — the phrase originates in Merezhkovsky’s novel, not with Leonardo.
source.excerptNote: Freud’s actual words, describing Leonardo in the third person. The circulating “I awoke, only to find that the rest of the world is still asleep” recasts this outside observation as a first-person boast Leonardo never made.

source.rightsNote: The exact first-person wording is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable author or source, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. The underlying third-person simile appeared in Freud’s essay (German 1910, English 1916) and, earlier, in Merezhkovsky’s novel (1900–1901) — but the circulating quote matches neither text verbatim.

author.name: Sigmund Freud
author.heading: Whose words these actually are
author.metaLine: 1856–1939 · Founder of psychoanalysis · after Dmitry Merezhkovsky
author.bio: Sigmund Freud (1856–1939), the founder of psychoanalysis, published Leonardo da Vinci and a Memory of His Childhood in 1910. In it he cast Leonardo as a mind out of step with his era — “like a man who awoke too early in the darkness, while the others were all still asleep” — a simile he attributed to the Russian Silver Age novelist Dmitry Merezhkovsky, whose The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci Freud counted among his favorite books. The internet later collapsed this outsider’s observation into a first-person line and pinned it on Leonardo himself.

cite.sourceCitation: Sigmund Freud, Leonardo da Vinci and a Memory of His Childhood (1910; English translation, 1916), crediting the simile to Dmitry Merezhkovsky, The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci (1900–1901). No such line appears in Leonardo da Vinci’s own writings.

misattribution.heading: How Freud’s simile became Leonardo’s ‘quote’
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook ‘magnet-name’ misattribution: a striking image written about Leonardo by someone else, decades after his death, rewritten in the first person and stamped with his name.

items.why: The line is absent from Leonardo’s notebooks and manuscripts. In a 2019 Check Your Fact review, Leonardo scholar Martin Kemp stated it is not among Leonardo’s genuine words.
The circulating first-person sentence is a rewrite of Freud’s third-person simile; it appears verbatim in neither Freud’s essay nor Merezhkovsky’s novel.

misattribution.truthLine: The real image is Freud’s, borrowed from Merezhkovsky — a description of Leonardo, not a boast by him.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Leonardo
lead: The line flatters exactly the myth we hold about Leonardo — the lone genius centuries ahead of everyone else — so it reads as something he might plausibly have thought. That plausibility, plus a famous name, is all a quote needs to spread.

Ironically, the sentiment is rooted in real writing about Leonardo: Freud’s 1910 psychoanalytic study reached for a Merezhkovsky simile to capture Leonardo’s isolation. What began as an outsider’s interpretation hardened, online, into a first-person motto.
context.pull: A description of Leonardo, rewritten as a quote by Leonardo.
